answer_text:
Yes. Let

\[
e(x):=2g(2x)-g(x).
\]

Then by hypothesis,

\[
e(x)\to 0 \qquad (x\to+\infty).
\]

From \(e(y/2)=2g(y)-g(y/2)\), we get

\[
g(y)=\frac12 g\!\left(\frac y2\right)+\frac12 e\!\left(\frac y2\right).
\]

Iterating this \(n\) times gives

\[
g(y)=2^{-n}g\!\left(\frac y{2^n}\right)
+\sum_{j=1}^n 2^{-j}e\!\left(\frac y{2^j}\right).
\tag{1}
\]

Now fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(e(x)\to 0\), choose \(A>0\) such that

\[
|e(t)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2} \qquad \text{for all } t\ge A.
\]

By local boundedness of \(g\), \(g\) is bounded on \([A,2A]\); set

\[
B:=\sup_{t\in[A,2A]} g(t)<\infty.
\]

For \(y\ge A\), choose

\[
n=\left\lfloor \log_2\frac{y}{A}\right\rfloor.
\]

Then

\[
A\le \frac{y}{2^n}<2A,
\]

and for every \(1\le j\le n\),

\[
\frac{y}{2^j}\ge \frac{y}{2^n}\ge A.
\]

Therefore \(|e(y/2^j)|<\varepsilon/2\) for all \(j=1,\dots,n\). Using (1),

\[
\begin{aligned}
g(y)
&=2^{-n}g\!\left(\frac y{2^n}\right)
+\sum_{j=1}^n 2^{-j}e\!\left(\frac y{2^j}\right)\\
&\le B\,2^{-n}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\sum_{j=1}^n 2^{-j}\\
&< B\,2^{-n}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\frac{y}{2^n}<2A\), we have \(2^{-n}<\frac{2A}{y}\). Hence

\[
g(y)<\frac{2AB}{y}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Choosing \(y\) sufficiently large makes \(\frac{2AB}{y}\le \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\), so for all large \(y\),

\[
0\le g(y)<\varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon>0\) was arbitrary, it follows that

\[
\lim_{x\to+\infty} g(x)=0.
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, it follows that } \lim_{x\to+\infty} g(x)=0.}
\]
